title: Seat Every Pair Side by Side
statement:
A row of 2n seats is grouped into n two-seat benches: seats 0 and 1 are the first bench, 2 and 3 the second, and so on. row[i] is the person in seat i; the people are numbered 0 to 2n − 1.

People come in pairs: 0 with 1, 2 with 3, and so on (person x's partner is x XOR 1). In one swap, any two people trade seats. Return the fewest swaps needed so that every pair shares a bench. Which bench a pair ends up on does not matter, nor the order within the bench.

examples.why: Swap persons 2 and 1: the benches become (0, 1) and (2, 3).
Pair 2–3 shares the first bench and pair 0–1 the second; order inside a bench does not matter.
All three benches are wrong, but they form one loop of three benches, and fixing a loop of k benches takes k − 1 swaps.

constraints: row is a permutation of 0 … row.length − 1
hints: Go bench by bench from the left. If the person in the first seat is not sitting with their partner, is there any harm in swapping the partner into the second seat right away?
That greedy swap fixes one bench for good and never undoes earlier work. To make it fast, keep a map from person to seat.
Graph view: make each bench a node and join the two benches that each pair is split across. Each connected loop of k benches needs exactly k − 1 swaps, so the answer is n minus the number of loops.

explain.intuition:
Treat each bench as a node. For every pair, draw an edge between the bench of one partner and the bench of the other (a pair already together gives a self-loop). Every bench holds two people, so every node has exactly two edge ends: the graph splits into separate cycles. A swap that seats one pair together cuts one bench out of its cycle, so a cycle of k benches needs k − 1 swaps, and no swap can do better than one bench per step. The answer is n − (number of cycles).

The greedy version reaches the same count without building the graph: for each bench in order, if the second seat does not hold the first person's partner, swap the partner in. A position map makes each swap O(1). It is like reordering items with drag-and-drop where every drop must land one item in its final place.
steps: For each bench start i = 0, 2, 4, …: let want = row[i] ^ 1.
If row[i + 1] !== want: let j = seat[want], swap row[i + 1] and row[j], update both entries in seat, and count one swap.
pitfalls: Counting the benches that are wrong. In [0, 3, 5, 2, 4, 1] all 3 are wrong but 2 swaps suffice.
Finding the partner with a linear search each time, which makes the greedy O(n²).
Forgetting to update the position map for the person who moved out of seat i + 1.

solutions.title: Greedy with a linear partner search
solutions.idea: Fix benches from left to right, scanning the rest of the row for the missing partner.

solutions.title: Greedy with a seat map
solutions.idea: Same left-to-right fix, but a person → seat array finds the partner in O(1).

solutions.title: Union-find over benches
solutions.idea: Join the two benches each pair is split across. Every component is a cycle needing size − 1 swaps, so the answer is n − components.

followups: Prove that the greedy left-to-right swap is never worse than any other first move.
Groups now have three members and benches three seats. Does the cycle argument still give the answer?
